MR.Guide.Heading: How to play
MR.Guide.Lead: Follow is a group story with no game master: one quest, one fellowship and three challenges. Here is each phase in short, with what you do and why. The full rules are in the book.
MR.Guide.basics.Title: Before you start
MR.Guide.basics.Why: Nobody runs the game: decisions are made as a group and the app keeps track.
MR.Guide.basics.Step1: Play by talking, on voice or at the table. Here you note what matters and draw the stones; no need to write the whole story.
MR.Guide.basics.Step2: The coloured strip at the top always says whose turn it is and what to do. If it says “Your turn”, it's you.
MR.Guide.basics.Step3: There is one shared sheet (the fellowship) and one sheet per character. Only you edit yours.
MR.Guide.basics.Step4: Dice fill a field with an idea. They are inspiration and never decide anything: change what you don't like.
MR.Guide.basics.Step5: Foundry needs a GM connected to save. That person plays like everyone else; they don't run the game.
MR.Guide.basics.Step6: Before you start, visit “Comfort” and note lines (what won't appear) and veils (what happens off screen).
MR.Guide.setup.Title: The quest
MR.Guide.setup.Why: Gets everyone agreeing on what you're after, in what world and what makes it hard, before anyone is created.
MR.Guide.setup.Now: Read the intro, customise the quest by answering the questions and pick two difficulties.
MR.Guide.setup.Step2: Answer the questions together to customise the quest. Note what you want to remember.
MR.Guide.setup.Step3: Pick two things that make the quest hard, from the list or your own. They set the scene and may inspire challenges.
MR.Guide.setup.Step4: If you like, rewrite the goal in your own words. Then press “Form the fellowship”.
MR.Guide.setup.Step5: From here on the quest lists are just inspiration: what matters is what you chose.
MR.Guide.characters.Title: The fellowship
MR.Guide.characters.Why: Each player has a main character and a supporting character. The story centres on the main characters and what they want from each other.
MR.Guide.characters.Now: Everyone fills in their main and supporting character sheets and marks “I'm ready”. Talk through your choices aloud.
MR.Guide.characters.Step1: Main character: name and concept (their role in the fellowship). They must want the quest to succeed, even if that changes later.
MR.Guide.characters.Step2: What I want from the quest: why your character is here. It can't match anyone else's.
MR.Guide.characters.Step3: What I want from you: something important you want from the main character on your left, who won't give it. Agree the why with that player: it's the tension you want to explore.
MR.Guide.characters.Step4: Supporting character: name, concept and a short description. Best if they relate to a main character across the table, not yours.
MR.Guide.characters.Step5: What you want is just a starting point: it can change or be dropped during play.
MR.Guide.choose.Title: Starting a challenge
MR.Guide.choose.Why: Each challenge is the next big step towards the goal. There are three; the third decides the quest and the first two change its odds.
MR.Guide.choose.Now: Someone who hasn't picked yet chooses the challenge, explains why it's hard and decides which main character opens it. Decide the pace as a group.
MR.Guide.choose.Step1: Someone who hasn't picked before chooses. It can be any challenge from the quest, even one already played. If unsure: what would we need to do now?
MR.Guide.choose.Step2: They explain what makes it hard and why it must be solved, without saying how it's overcome.
MR.Guide.choose.Step3: They decide which main character would take the initiative. Not their own. That player sets the first scene.
MR.Guide.choose.Step4: Together, decide the pace: minutes, hours, days, weeks, months or years.
MR.Guide.choose.Step5: Once chosen, the challenge is a fact. Characters may refuse it, but that brings you closer to failure.
MR.Guide.scenes.Title: Scenes
MR.Guide.scenes.Why: They explore how the characters deal with the challenge and with each other. They don't decide whether it's overcome: the stones do.
MR.Guide.scenes.Now: Each person sets one scene in turn, going left: who is there, where and what is happening. Then you play it by talking.
MR.Guide.scenes.Step1: Say who is there, where and what is happening. Your main character is present and it's their moment; leave your supporting character out.
MR.Guide.scenes.Step2: Two or three characters is ideal. You can invent outsiders and ask others to play them.
MR.Guide.scenes.Step3: Everyone controls their own characters: to do something to someone else's, describe the effect you want and they decide.
MR.Guide.scenes.Step4: If someone had it too easy, anyone can add a consequence. If it affects another player's character, negotiate it.
MR.Guide.scenes.Step5: Never narrate the challenge's success or failure. Cut early: whoever set the scene decides when it ends.
MR.Guide.stones.Title: The stones
MR.Guide.stones.Why: They mix what the characters feel and what you think as players. Nobody controls the outcome alone.
MR.Guide.stones.Now: Everyone chooses stones in secret. Once all are in, they're shown, the red ones are explained and two are drawn.
MR.Guide.stones.Step1: The bowl starts with 1 white and 1 red. In the third challenge, also add 1 white per challenge won and 1 red per challenge lost.
MR.Guide.stones.Step2: For your main character: if they're not happy with the fellowship's path, 1 red; if they want the quest to fail, 2 red; otherwise none.
MR.Guide.stones.Step3: As a player: if you think the fellowship did what it needed to, 1 white; if not, 1 red.
MR.Guide.stones.Step4: Show them all at once. Anyone who added red for their character briefly explains why.
MR.Guide.stones.Step5: Draw two without looking. The first is about the fellowship, the second about the challenge.
MR.Guide.outcome.Title: The outcome
MR.Guide.outcome.Why: The two stones say whether you overcome the challenge and whether the fellowship loses someone. Then you narrate it together.
MR.Guide.outcome.Now: Narrate how the challenge ends. If there's a loss, decide together who leaves the story and how.
MR.Guide.outcome.Step1: White, white: success. Red, white: you overcome the challenge but lose a character.
MR.Guide.outcome.Step2: White, red: you lose a character and fail. Red, red: betrayal, you lose a character and fail.
MR.Guide.outcome.Step3: The loss can be a main or supporting character; their player decides how. If you can't agree, one of the picker's characters is lost.
MR.Guide.outcome.Step4: Nobody is out: lose your main and your supporting character steps up; if you have none, adopt someone else's or introduce a newcomer.
MR.Guide.epilogue.Title: The epilogue
MR.Guide.epilogue.Why: After three challenges the quest ends. Glimpse the characters' lives: was it worth it?
MR.Guide.epilogue.Now: Everyone briefly narrates what became of their main character. Then close the story.
MR.Guide.epilogue.Step1: Tell your main character's life after the quest and whether they think it was worth it.
MR.Guide.epilogue.Step2: If you lost them right at the end, you can narrate their legacy or memory.
MR.Guide.epilogue.Step3: Press “Close the story” to see the printable credits.
MR.Challenge.LeadHelp: Whoever would take the initiative on this problem. Not your own. Their player sets the first scene.
MR.Settings.PhaseGuideHint: Shows on the shared sheet what to do now and why it matters.
MR.Challenge.TimescaleHelp: Decide as a group, so every scene fits that time.
MR.Error.LeadNotOwn: Whoever picks the challenge can't choose their own character to open it.
MR.Error.NeedTimescale: Decide the pace of the challenge first.
MR.Stones.RevealHelp: Anyone who added red stones for their character briefly explains why. Then draw two: the first is about the fellowship, the second about the challenge.
MR.Quest.GenreHelp: Decides which tables the inspiration dice use (names, places, situations…) when the quest has no options of its own.
MR.Quest.ThemeHelp: Only changes the sheet colours. Pick the one that best conveys the tone.
MR.Quest.Field.title.Label: Title
MR.Quest.Field.title.Help: A short, recognisable name, like a film title. It's what shows in the lobby and the credits.
MR.Quest.Field.tagline.Label: Tagline
MR.Quest.Field.tagline.Help: A single line that sells the quest: the place or situation plus a hint of threat. Helps choose between quests at a glance.
MR.Quest.Field.intro.Label: Introduction
MR.Quest.Field.intro.Help: Two to four sentences read aloud at the start: who you are as a group, what is happening and what's at stake. Set up the situation, not the ending, and leave details open for the questions.
MR.Quest.Field.goal.Label: Goal
MR.Quest.Field.goal.Help: One sentence with a clear verb saying what counts as success, so that after the third challenge you know whether it was achieved. Everyone pursues it, each for their own reasons.
MR.Quest.Field.questions.Label: Questions to customise
MR.Quest.Field.questions.Help: Open questions the group answers together before making characters: era, place, who's in charge, what exactly the problem is. They let the table make the quest its own; best if they offer several options and have no right answer.
MR.Quest.Field.difficulties.Label: What makes the quest hard
MR.Quest.Field.difficulties.Help: Background obstacles weighing on the whole quest (lack of time, a powerful enemy, internal mistrust…), not specific challenges. The group picks two, so you need at least two; six gives a real choice. Mix them: external, internal, environmental.
MR.Quest.Field.concepts.Label: Character concepts
MR.Quest.Field.concepts.Help: Roles within the fellowship in two or three words (a trade, a rank, a relationship to the group). They should fit the goal and give distinct profiles, including someone awkward or an outsider. At least six, one per player at a full table.
MR.Quest.Field.desires.Label: What I want from the quest
MR.Quest.Field.desires.Help: Personal reasons for being on the quest: what each character gains if it succeeds or from how it's done (fame, revenge, protecting someone…). Best if they clash, because that creates tension inside the group. At least six: no two characters may want the same.
MR.Quest.Field.wants.Label: What I want from you, but you won't give me
MR.Quest.Field.wants.Help: Kinds of complicated relationship between two characters: something one needs from the other, who denies it (trust, forgiveness, recognition…). Write the category and, if you like, a nuance. These relationships drive the scenes. At least three; players may share them.
MR.Quest.Field.challenges.Label: Challenges
MR.Quest.Field.challenges.Help: Important steps towards the goal, written as tasks (“Get…”, “Escape from…”). Mix preparation, confrontation and twists so each session follows a different arc. Format: “Title — why it's hard”. Three are played and may repeat, but eight gives variety.

MR.Settings.PortalFxHint: Glow, particles and light for the setting in the room's portal. Turn them off if you change the background image or don't want them.

MR.Portal.NotOnStage: Open the “MR · Story Night” scene to see the preview while you adjust.

MR.Portal.ZoneHelp: While you adjust, the scene shows a white outline. Line it up with the portal opening and save.
